title: Health readings from a wearable
like: private health summaries from a wrist device
brief: A wearable records health readings even when its phone or cloud service is unavailable. Keep raw readings on the device when possible and upload only consented summaries in sparse batches. The system must not lose locally saved readings during a supported outage, and deleting an account must have a verifiable end-to-end workflow.

clarify.q: Is this an emergency alert service?
clarify.a: No. It is a retrospective personal dashboard. Local trends remain available offline; the cloud must not be presented as a safety-critical alarm path. A medical alarm would require different guarantees.

clarify.q: What is stored locally and for how long?
clarify.a: Assume one 16-byte reading each second, with a durable encrypted local log. Reserve at least 30 days of raw capacity, including overhead and a safety margin. A 14-day phone or cloud outage must not lose readings already durably saved, provided the device remains intact and has power.

Only an opt-in daily encrypted 1 KB summary by default, plus explicit user-selected exports. Derive the summary locally. The service has routing metadata but not health-content keys. No raw content in analytics, logs or push payloads.

clarify.q: What if there is no space or a device is lost?
clarify.a: Never silently claim a saved reading when the log is full or not durable. Warn before the supported reserve is exhausted and state the retention policy. Device destruction before an authorized backup is outside the no-loss promise. Recovery and revocation need an explicit key policy.

notes: Local raw readings are 16 B each at one reading per second. Reserve at least 30 days of local raw capacity for the supported 14-day outage. Each of 100,000 opted-in devices uploads at most one 1 KB summary per day; raw readings remain local (approx.).

Cloud peak is a reconnect burst. Use the peak and mix to separate summary ingestion, account reads and wake requests. The daily curve is a conservative capacity drill, separate from the sparse average billing forecast.
The scored no-loss target concerns acknowledged cloud summaries. The device log, fourteen-day outage reserve, consent, encryption keys and proof of deletion are worked protocol obligations.
The sender target concerns push acceptance only. No cloud availability percentage is a guarantee of medical safety or survival of a destroyed device.
Sources emit only their assigned request types. The source rates below reproduce the aggregate workload; protocol guarantees still require the separate design checkpoint.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

workloadPlan.role: consented encrypted summaries; raw log is local

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Fourteen-day local raw payload
numbers.how: 16 B/s × 86,400 × 14 ÷ 1,000,000; reserve more for encryption, indexing and margin (approx.).

numbers.label: Raw payload per day
numbers.how: 16 B × 86,400 readings/day; compared with one 1 KB daily summary (approx.).

hints: Separate local capture, phone relay and cloud acceptance. Which promise applies while the radio is off?
Persist a monotonic device sequence and outbox locally, checkpoint only durable summaries, and retry stable batch ids. Keep raw content out of cloud telemetry.

Use local encrypted logging and on-device summaries, then a jittered authenticated API to a durable key-value store. Budget 30-day device storage, explicit consent, enrollment and recovery keys, deletion receipts and restore checks.

editorial.summary: Persist readings in a durable local encrypted log with sequence numbers, checksums and crash recovery. Derive summaries on the device and place consented encrypted uploads in a local outbox. A phone can relay ciphertext without treating the cloud as the capture path. The API authenticates device identity, deduplicates batch sequence ranges and stores ciphertext summaries. The graph begins at optional cloud uploads; it cannot prove the local capture or encryption promises.

designs.name: Device-owned readings and sparse encrypted summaries
designs.why: The key-value store fits immutable device-and-date summary keys and small reads. The API validates consent and stable upload identities; storage operations enforce uniqueness and monotonic sequence acknowledgement. KMS protects server account metadata only. Push contains a wake hint without health content. The steady cloud drill deliberately tests more activity than the normal sparse schedule, so its projected bill is a capacity exercise.

tradeoffs: Thirty days of one 16-byte sample/s is about 41.5 MB payload. Reserve extra for authenticated-encryption tags, indexes, crash-safe metadata and compaction. Do not confuse payload with safe device capacity.

A saved local reading is protected against the stated software/network outage, not device destruction, power loss before flush or an unbounded disconnection. Define flush semantics and a visible low-space response.

Daily 1 KB summaries minimize upload compared with about 1.38 MB/day raw data, but lose server-side detail and still reveal sensitive health trends. Optional exports require separate consent and expiry.
Use device sequence order for deduplication; record capture-time uncertainty when clocks change. A late upload must not replace a newer summary without a version rule.

Revocation stops future authorized sync, not already copied plaintext. Deletion tracks active summaries, versions, caches, exports and backups, and restores must reapply deletion records before serving. Recovery cannot secretly bypass end-to-end content keys. A disconnected device cannot receive a deletion command immediately. Erase managed cloud copies on the stated schedule, reject revoked device uploads, and state that endpoint deletion awaits reconnection or local action.
editorial.realWorld: For 100,000 devices, one daily 1 KB summary is about 100 MB/day cloud payload. Uploading all assumed raw readings would be about 138 GB/day before overhead. Radio wakeups and tail energy matter as well as bytes, so batch uploads and measure on real devices (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Health readings from a wearable: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A durable copy across the required failure boundary before acknowledgement
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.
